newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Deeper Europe, Asia ties stalled over Timor, Burma.
newsitem.headline: Deeper Europe, Asia ties stalled over Timor, Burma.

text.p: Moves to deepen ties between Europe and Southeast Asia stalled on Wednesday over how to deal with Burma and East Timor, delegates said.

They said senior officials from the 15-nation European Union and the seven members of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) could not agree on wording for a final declaration that indirectly deals with the thorny issues.

They said the major topic at the preparatory meeting for two days of ministerial discussions on Thursday and Friday was Burma, but the fight between Portugal and Indonesia over East Timor was the major stumbling block.

"The Portuguese will not agree any declaration that could bind them to extending relations with Indonesia or ASEAN while perceived human rights problems in East Timor remain unresolved," said an EU official who declined to be identified.
"There are some sticking points which they would present to the ministers," ASEAN Secretary-General Ajit Singh told reporters at the end of the senior officials meeting.
"The disagreements are on both political and economic issues," Singh said.

Indonesia invaded the former Portuguese colony of East Timor in 1975 after a civil war following Lisbon's abrupt decolonisation. Up to a third of the population died in the famine and fighting that followed.
But the single biggest topic of debate on Wednesday was Burma, which has been promised ASEAN membership along with Laos and Cambodia, possibly as early as this year, delegates said.
ASEAN groups Indonesia, Malaysia, Brunei, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
The officials talked about Burma for about two-and-a-half hours, Philippine Foreign Affairs Undersecretary Rodolfo Severino told reporters.

The London-based human rights group Amnesty International said on Wednesday political repression and human rights violations in Burma last year reached their highest levels since the suppression of a popular uprising at the end of the 1980s.
An Amnesty report called on ASEAN to end its policy of "constructive engagement" with Rangoon. ASEAN officials have said repeatedly they believe their policy to be right.
Burma's military government dismissed the scathing Amnesty report as "ridiculous", and called it propaganda for anti-Burmese organisations.
A reference to Burma, along with East Timor, in the final conference declaration in Singapore would be left to the ministers to decide, one ASEAN diplomat said.
The economic stakes in improving ties between the two regions are enormous.

ASEAN was the EU's second largest export market in 1995 and third largest trading partner after Japan and the United States. The EU is the second largest investor after Japan in ASEAN, whose combined population of 400 million represents a potential market larger than Europe.

But ASEAN diplomats remain adamant that their policy of "constructive engagement" with Rangoon is effective and express impatience with Western pressure on subjects they consider internal to the grouping.
"We cannot have a Southeast Asia that is divided between an ASEAN Southeast Asia and a non-ASEAN Southeast Asia," Severino said.

The issue of Burma's membership is particularly vexing as the European parliament has repeatedly warned the European Commission -- the EU's executive -- that it will not tolerate dealings with Rangoon.
